tr.td: Serene, a company town around the Columbine Mine in Weld County, Colorado
Armed state police and mine guards fired into a crowd of striking coal miners and their families
No police officer or guard was ever held to account; the mine's owner later signed a contract with the United Mine Workers
Rocky Mountain Fuel Company, whose largest stockholder was Josephine Roche
Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), known as the Wobblies
About 500 according to several accounts; one history gives 500 to 600
Counts differ: about 20, 23, 36 and "more than sixty", depending on the source
Rifles and tear gas; strikers and several later accounts say at least two machine guns
Rocks; the IWW's standing instruction was to leave guns at home or at the union hall

content.p: Before sunrise on 21 November 1927, several hundred striking coal miners, many of them with their wives and children, walked up to the gate of Serene, a fenced and guarded company town in northern Colorado. Within minutes, armed men on the other side had shot into the crowd. Six miners died, and dozens more were wounded. None of the people who fired was punished.

The shooting is known as the Columbine Mine massacre, after the pit that the town existed to serve. It came thirteen years after the Ludlow killings in the southern coalfields and has been far less remembered. A historian who wrote a doctoral dissertation on the strike calls it understudied and asks why Ludlow is remembered and Columbine largely forgotten.
content.h2: A strike that grew out of a protest
content.p: By 1927 Colorado's coal miners had little to show for fifty years of strikes and confrontations. Libcom's account describes deadly accidents (121 men killed at Hastings in 1917, 31 at Oakdale and Empire in 1919, 27 at Sopris and Southwestern in 1922 and 1923) and pay in scrip that could be spent only at the company store. Miners bought their own tools and blasting powder and were not paid for "dead work" such as timbering. A local history adds that shifts of ten to twelve hours, six days a week, had hardly changed since Ludlow.

The United Mine Workers, who had led the Ludlow strike, had by then lost their footing in the state. The Industrial Workers of the World moved into the gap. Many Colorado miners first walked out for a few days in sympathy with the Sacco and Vanzetti general strike called by the IWW, after the two anarchists were executed in August 1927. The union then turned that discontent into a coal strike. Sources disagree on the start: Libcom and a Deadly Events summary give 18 October, while the Lafayette local history says miners around Lafayette, Louisville and Superior began walking out on 8 October.

The owners would not deal. They refused to recognise the IWW and, according to the local history, called its organisers "crooks", "Reds" and "imported trouble-makers". Governor Adams and most newspapers sided with them, and the governor declared the strike illegal. In the south, the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company bargained with its company union, which was granted a raise of 68 cents a day and passed a resolution to dismiss any IWW members on the payroll. Rebel Graphics, an IWW-sympathetic site, reports that this raise was withdrawn in 1931.
Libcom counts 113 mines closed across the state, 13 still running and about 8,400 men on strike. In the north the one big exception was the Columbine.

The Columbine Mine opened in 1914 and sat about five miles northeast of Lafayette. It belonged to the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company, as did Serene itself. The company, Libcom and Rebel Graphics report, kept the pit running with about 150 strikebreakers, lured by a raise of fifty cents a day. The Lafayette history says that soon after the strike began a barbed-wire wall went up around the whole town, with two gates, and that a searchlight on the tipple swept the ground all night while armed guards patrolled around the clock.

Each day picketers made the rounds of the other local mines, then gathered at Serene. Between 500 and 1,200 strikers and family members came on busy days, the same history says. Newspapers dwelt on the foreign origins of the strikers, most of them, one paper said, Bulgarians, Mexicans, Greeks and Italians, and one newspaper mocked IWW leaders as "tramps with their pants pressed". Rebel Graphics adds that two local papers openly urged the state to use force and that National Guard aircraft made mock dives at union rallies.

Tension climbed through November. Pickets crowded the roads on 7 November and the mine briefly closed. On 12 November, 500 to 600 strikers rushed the upper gate and paraded through the town. Two days later, six officers who tried to arrest strike leaders were beaten. Governor Adams then warned that guards had orders to shoot if the property was invaded again, and two machine guns were set up inside the town, one on the water tank and one on the tipple, according to the Lafayette history. Rebel Graphics quotes a Boulder Daily Camera headline of the same week saying that machine guns "are the best answer to the picketers".
content.h2: The owner who gave out doughnuts
content.p: The company's largest shareholder was Josephine Roche, who inherited her father's shares in January 1927. The Denver Public Library records that he had often used his influence against unions, and that Roche was "a very different person". A former Denver policewoman and juvenile-court worker, she had pledged to reform coal-mining conditions in Colorado. The library says she ordered coffee and doughnuts handed out to the strikers.

She did not control the company outright at that time, Rebel Graphics notes, and in its account other operators worked behind the scenes toward a confrontation that would bring in the state's militia. That is the website's claim; the pages consulted do not document who, if anyone, planned it. In a 1944 memorandum, the same page reports, Roche blamed the Colorado Fuel and Iron official Jesse Welborn as chiefly responsible for the circumstances that led to the shooting.

The state's chief law-enforcement officer on the ground was Louis Scherf, who, according to the Lafayette history, called out every available man to Serene that morning, reportedly on a tip. Before dawn the strikers picketed the nearby Morrison, Puritan and State mines and then walked to Serene. About 500 reached the gates by Libcom's count, and the Lafayette history gives 500 to 600.

What followed is told in several versions. Rebel Graphics describes two deputy sheriffs warning the crowd off the property, then a group of heavily armed men in civilian clothes behind the gate. Scherf shouted, "Who are your leaders?" and the answer came back, "We're all leaders!" One of the police is quoted as saying: "If you want to come in here, come ahead, but we'll carry you out."

A scuffle broke out. Most accounts agree that Adam Bell, the IWW organiser for the Boulder area, was hit on the head. The Lafayette history records a competing popular story in which a woman carrying a flag, Mrs. Beranek, was clubbed, and notes that the guards' version, the one the newspapers printed, had Bell approaching alone and ignoring warning shots. That history concludes that most likely there was a general charge down the lane. Whichever it was, the strikers surged through the gate. Libcom says tear gas was fired, and that strikers threw rocks and hurled canisters back.

The police then fell back about a hundred yards and fired. Libcom reports rifles and at least two machine guns, with strikers later saying a third gun on the tipple caught them in a crossfire. The Lafayette history notes that the newspapers wrote only that strikers "claim" machine guns were used, and that the guards said they used only rifles, but that the people interviewed for its account agreed there was "no doubt" at least one machine gun fired. A reference work cited by Deadly Events states that the Rangers denied it, yet "testimony is clear" that machine guns were used. One of the local-history witnesses, who was approaching the scene on foot, said you can tell machine-gun fire from rifle fire by sound.

All accounts agree on six dead. The Lafayette history says three died at the scene or within minutes and two more within 48 hours, and that Mike Ridovich held on until 29 November. The memorial stone in Lafayette Cemetery gives the names of five: Jerry Davis, John Eastenes, Frank Kovich, Nick Spanudakhis and Mike Vidovich. The sixth, Rene Jacques, was buried in Louisville.

The wounded are counted differently. Deadly Events quotes a summary of 20, another passage in the same page 36, Westword 23 and Libcom and Rebel Graphics "more than sixty". The LAWCHA historian writes that the number is disputed to this day, and the Lafayette history says 23 were hurt badly enough to be taken to hospitals, mostly in Longmont. A woman in miner's overalls was among them and survived after days near death.

No guard or police officer was reported shot. Rebel Graphics and Deadly Events both connect this to the miners' lack of weapons, and the latter says they had been told to leave any at the union hall in Erie. The Lafayette history says the guards claimed rocks were thrown and warning shots fired, but notes that no guard was hurt, so the stones cannot have done much.

The Lafayette history records that the governor angrily put the blame on the strikers, imposed martial law and sent in the National Guard. The militia sent to Serene was made up of three companies from Fort Collins, Loveland and Denver, mostly young men who were students, whom newspapers called "student soldiers". At a meeting in Erie that noon, strikers talked of taking over the Columbine, but an IWW leader known as "Duke", who had urged action the day before, talked them out of it. A mass funeral for four of the dead took place at Lafayette a few days later, and on 26 November a protest of about 300 people in New York's Union Square was held back by 160 police.

The violence did not stop. According to Libcom, two strikers were killed at Walsenburg two weeks later. A reference work cited by Deadly Events describes a raid on the IWW hall there on 12 January 1928 that left two members dead. The strike, as the Lafayette history sees it, then petered out, and known IWW men were blacklisted in the mining camps. Libcom says the IWW's backing in the Colorado mines had been broken.

For the company, the shooting turned out to be a turning point. Rebel Graphics says Roche, once she had control, declared it was time to recognise a union, though not the IWW, and Libcom writes that she ended the strike weeks later by affiliating the company union with the American Federation of Labor and eventually recognising the United Mine Workers. LAWCHA's account gives the date of the contract as 1928, and says it helped rescue United Mine Workers president John L. Lewis after a strike elsewhere had ended in defeat. Roche made the Ludlow strike leader John Lawson her vice president. Her later career included running for governor in 1934 and a federal public-health post under Franklin Roosevelt.

The IWW got no contract. Libcom states that no militia member or police officer was ever held accountable. A reference work cited by Deadly Events adds that lawsuits against the governor, the Rangers and the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company were dismissed in 1932.

Serene outlived the strike. The Lafayette history says the town grew to about 2,000 people and that the Columbine mine remained a major producer until it closed in 1945, the last mine the company shut in Colorado. The town was demolished in 1972 and 1973.

The site now lies, the LAWCHA historian writes, under a landfill, near a golf-course housing development in Erie. A memorial stone in Lafayette Cemetery marks the five graves, and Westword describes a rest area and memorial sign on State Highway 7. The sign, quoted by Deadly Events, says the miners' sacrifice "manifested the struggle for the rights and dignity of all Colorado coal miners."
